phase1.intro:
Every window you've built so far has been hand-nailed together in Java. FXML is the alternative.

Where should we start?

dialogue: FXML is exactly what the name says: [[term:F]]X [[term:M]]ark[[term:L]]anguage — an XML dialect where each tag is a JavaFX class (`<VBox>`, `<Button>`, `<Label>`) and each attribute is a property. A [[term:FXMLLoader]] reads that file at runtime and builds the exact same scene graph you'd build by hand.

stickyNote.flavor: 📄 the layout as a file, not Java code
stickyNote.definition: FXML is an XML dialect where tags map to JavaFX classes and attributes map to properties. FXMLLoader reads it and builds the same scene graph.

topics.buttonText: What's the actual benefit of splitting layout from logic?
dialogue: Your layout lives in one file, your logic lives in a separate [[term:controller]] class, connected by [[term:@FXML]]. [[key:That split means a designer can rearrange the window without touching a line of Java, and a developer can rewrite behavior without touching the layout]] — the same separation encapsulation gave you in Unit 1, applied to UI.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔀 layout and logic in separate files
stickyNote.definition: FXML holds layout; a controller class holds logic, connected via @FXML. This lets layout and behavior change independently.

dialogue: [[term:Scene Builder]] is Oracle's drag-and-drop tool for editing FXML visually instead of hand-typing tags — [[fun:it generates the exact same FXML file a human would write by hand]], it's purely a convenience layer, not a separate technology.

stickyNote.definition: Scene Builder is a drag-and-drop visual editor that generates the same FXML a human would hand-write — a convenience layer, not a new technology.

phase1.openingDialogue: FXML describes layout as a separate file instead of Java code — separating layout from logic, editable by hand or via Scene Builder. 📄

phase2.explanation:
No broken code — conceptual lesson. Two misconceptions worth clearing up before we wire up a real controller next lesson.

"FXML replaces Java code" — [[warn:not quite]]. FXML replaces the *construction* code — the new Label(), getChildren().add() calls — but you still write a Java controller class for behavior (what happens on a click, how data gets validated). FXML and Java split the job; neither replaces the other.

"You need Scene Builder to use FXML" — also not true. [[key:FXML is just a text file]]; you can write it by hand in any editor, the same way you could hand-write HTML without a visual page builder. Scene Builder just makes the process faster and more visual — it's optional tooling, not a requirement of the format.

mcq.question:
Which statement about FXML is TRUE?

A) FXML files are written in HTML
B) The @FXML annotation is used to bind UI elements to controller fields
C) FXML can only be created with Scene Builder
D) FXML makes JavaFX applications slower

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:FXMLLoader builds the scene graph using reflection]] — it reads a tag like <Button text="OK"/>, looks up the javafx.scene.control.Button class by name, calls its no-arg constructor, and then calls the matching setText("OK") setter it finds by convention. That's the same reflective pattern PropertyValueFactory uses in TableView, coming up a couple lessons from now.
